speechtext:
Last evening, Mr. Chairman, at ten o'clock I was just drawing to a close on my remarks regarding this resolution. I have but one or two other things to say. When the United Kingdom government passed their bill relating to a health plan in 1948, and following the implementation of that legislation there, we in this country heard a great deal of adverse publicity about the operation of the scheme, the abuses which were taking place under it and the opposition to it by the medical profession and by others over there. It is reasonable to expect that sort of adverse publicity because it was something new; it was a drastic change from a system which they had in effect in Great Britain before that time. Usually any time there is a great change, in as much as we are conservative-minded,- and naturally I mean "conservative" with a small "c"-we are reluctant to accept it. There is a transitional period when a change takes place, and it takes time for us to get used to the change. That is one of the reasons why there was reluctance to accept the national health scheme in Great Britain, but it is not the only reason why all the adverse publicity was generated. I think I can say without fear of much contradiction, at least on the general principle of it, that the plan in effect in Great Britain now and for quite a number of years has become completely acceptable to
850	HOUSE OF
Hospital Insurance Act the general public, to the administrators and to the medical profession which opposed it in its early days.
If we in Canada enter into a similar type of an all-inclusive health scheme at this time, as we should, in participation with the provinces, I think we can expect a certain amount of prejudice and biased opposition to such a plan. We can also expect that most of that opposition and most of the complaints which would arise out of the establishment of such a plan would be unfair. We could expect complaints to be similar to those which I recall in the province of British Columbia, following the establishment there of a hospital insurance plan. I will agree, without any request, that there was a great deal of justification for the opposition to and the disagreement with the operation of the plan that we have in British Columbia, for the simple reason that it was put into effect as legislation, on the eve of a general election, as an election program without any planning, without any co-ordination, without any attempt to establish a proper administrative structure to deal with the act. That is the main reason why the feeling arose.
I think it is also true to say that if we establish such a plan as we in the C.C.F. have been propounding over the years, we can expect that there will be initially a heavy drain on public funds, on the public treasury, arising out of the operation of a national health plan. This would be for two reasons. The first reason is what we might call the natural tendency to abuse the plan itself. We in this country are conditioned to the theme of getting something for nothing, and we look upon the federal treasury or the provincial treasury or government institutions, especially in these fields, as providing us with something for nothing, not realizing, of course, that we pay for it in the first instance through taxation either directly or indirectly. But there would still be a tendency to take advantage of the facilities and services offered under such a health plan. That would be one reason why there would be a greater drain initially on the treasury than we might expect and greater than when the plan is established.
There is another reason why we could expect a heavy drain on the treasury initially. People who in past years could not or felt they could not afford to make necessary visits to a doctor or dentist in order to have an ailment diagnosed or dental work done will want to have it done. These people have put off such visits because they felt they could not afford to have these things done. They have said, "I will do it some other time.
I may have ulcers but right at the moment they are not bothering me too much. I need 

dental work done but I will put it off for another few months because I cannot afford it." If such a plan comes into effect there will be a backlog of work that people have needed to have done in years past but could not afford to have done. They will find that there is a chance to have it done at no immediate great cost to them other than their contribution through taxes toward the operation of the plan.
Actually I do not feel that the over-all cost of such an all-inclusive plan would be any greater than the amount of money that Canadians now spend on health care except during the initial period because of the two reasons I mentioned earlier. I believe as much money is spent now on private insurance coverage, doctors' services, dental and hospital care in those provinces where no plan is in effect. I do not believe that the total amount expended throughout the nation would be any greater than is being spent at the moment.
I realize that I have but a few minutes before my time expires and I should like to sum up briefly the attitude of the C.C.F. to the resolution and, in a broader sense, the necessity of instituting a national health plan. The original act introduced by the Liberal government was not good enough. It did not go far enough and its coverage was too restricted. Some changes have been made. Second, the resolution does not go far enough because all it means is six months additional coverage in some parts of the country. The action of the government now as found in the resolution is inconsistent with its pledges and election promises of a few months ago. An all-inclusive plan should be instituted now.
